questions.prompt: What is Record<Key, Value> most useful for?
options: Changing a type into a database table at runtime.
Guaranteeing that external input has been validated.
Describing an object mapping a set of keys to values of a consistent type.
questions.answer_key: Describing an object mapping a set of keys to values of a consistent type.
questions.explanation: Record creates a mapped object type; runtime contents still depend on the data and checks.

questions.prompt: Which statement is correct about “Index Signatures”?
options: The learner should publish hidden solutions so the exercise can grade itself.
The concept should be demonstrated with objects with dynamic keys and checked against its intended contract.
The safest approach is to skip diagnostics and trust the first output.
A type assertion automatically validates every value at runtime.
questions.answer_key: The concept should be demonstrated with objects with dynamic keys and checked against its intended contract.
questions.explanation: The supplied syllabus explicitly includes “Objects with dynamic keys”; connect it to a concrete example and verify the behavior relevant to this lesson.

questions.prompt: What is a good verification step after practicing “Index Signatures”?
options: Check string and number index signatures, include a meaningful failure case where appropriate, and document any runtime or version assumptions.
Assume index signatures and known properties is unnecessary because the code has type annotations.
Ignore compiler or test failures if the interface looks correct.
Treat passing a static token check as proof that the program executed correctly.
questions.answer_key: Check string and number index signatures, include a meaningful failure case where appropriate, and document any runtime or version assumptions.
questions.explanation: The syllabus includes “String and number index signatures”. Verification should match the concept: type-level checks, runtime tests, configuration checks or human review as appropriate.
